title: The boy who asked for nothing
hookLine: the man-lion offers Prahlada any boon, and he turns it down
carry: dharma-megha comes to one who wants no return
last: SEE THE SEER, AND THE EGO WINDS DOWN.

cards: The man-lion has burst out of the pillar, and the demon king is gone. But Narasimha's rage is so fierce that even the gods are afraid to go near him.
So they send a small boy: Prahlada, who never stopped remembering Vishnu. The lion's anger cools. He lays his hand on the child's head and says: ask me for anything.
And Prahlada, who came through poison and snakes for this god, says no. A servant who wants rewards from his master, he says, isn't a servant. He's a merchant.

teach.b: That's the Bhagavata Purana, and it sits right beside today's sutra. Sutra 4.29: prasankhyane 'py akusidasya sarvatha vivekakhyater dharmameghah samadhih.

teach.h: AKUSIDA: ONE WHO TAKES NO INTEREST.
teach.b: For one who takes no interest even in the highest knowledge, from discernment in every way, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma. The money word is kusida: lending at interest. An akusida charges none.

Prahlada would understand: no trading with what's holiest. Patanjali's yogi reaches the clearest seeing there is and doesn't try to collect on it. No powers, no status, not even keeping it as a trophy.
Earlier, Patanjali warned that the powers are obstacles, and that even an invitation from the gods mustn't stir attachment or pride. This is that refusal carried all the way up.
Yoga and bhakti, the path of devotion, are different roads, and they meet right here. When even that last wanting goes, what arrives is dharma-megha.
Megha is the heavy monsoon cloud. Commentators read the image two ways: a cloud that rains dharma on everything, or one that rains away the last of karma. Either way it isn't a prize.

teach.h: DHARMA-MEGHA COMES TO ONE WHO WANTS NO RETURN.
teach.b: The same name, dharma-megha, appears in Buddhist texts for the last stage of the bodhisattva's path: two neighbors reaching for the same cloud. And today?

Many Hindus make vows to God: I'll fast if I pass, I'll walk to the temple if she gets well. That's an honest kind of prayer, kept for generations. Prahlada points past it, to a love that has stopped keeping accounts.

how: In the Yoga tradition, dharma-megha samadhi is described as the last stage before kaivalya, reached only when the practitioner seeks nothing, not even from the highest discernment.

o: a lender who charges fair interest on loans
one who takes no interest, even on the highest seeing
a monsoon cloud that brings the year's rain

games.q: the boy and the cloud — tap the pairs.
p: the samadhi of the cloud of dharma

s: offered any boon, Prahlada asks for a kingdom
he says a servant who wants rewards from his master is a merchant, not a servant.
akusida comes from a word about money
kusida is lending at interest. the akusida takes no return, even on the highest discernment.
dharma-megha is a reward the yogi earns and keeps
it comes only when even that wanting is gone.

games.q: you've reached the clearest discernment there is. what does 4.29 say opens the cloud of dharma?
o: wanting nothing from it at all.
holding it tightly so it stays.
games.why: for one who takes no interest, even in the highest knowledge, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma.

practice: For these two minutes, keep no account: don't track how calm you are, or how well this is going. If you catch yourself scoring, smile at the scorekeeper and set the pencil down.
If you pray, offer the sit to God and ask for nothing back; if you don't, just breathe the way rain falls, not to get anything back.

wordCard.voice: Akusida, one who takes no interest. Dharma-megha samadhi comes to such a person, even at the highest discernment, wanting no return.

orig.note: Sanskrit dharma-megha: the cloud of dharma. megha is a rain cloud.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma-megha comes to one who wants no return. Prahlada asked for nothing. That's day four hundred eighty-seven.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 7.9–7.10 (Prahlada calms Narasimha; offered boons, he says a servant who wants rewards is a merchant, and asks that no desire arise in his heart)
Yoga Sutra 4.29 in full (prasaṃkhyāne 'py akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ)
Yoga Sutras 3.37 and 3.51 (powers as obstacles; the invitation of the gods refused)
Dashabhumika Sutra (dharmamegha as the tenth bhumi)
